2026-10-23 | Lab 9" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 css: contrast-slide-styling.css execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg --- ## Outline - `emmeans` with One-Way ANOVA - Pairwise comparisons - Contrasts ::: {.cell} ::: ## Lab 07 Follow-Up! ![](../media/lab_09/lab-07-mistake.png){fig-align="center"} I could have clarified this better: here, $95\%$ refers to a shorthand of $\pm 2 \ \text{SD}$ of the *prior distribution* for the intercept. I added a note for this on the slides as of 2026-10-23! # One-Way ANOVA Estimated Marginal Means ## Estimated Marginal Means EMMs, also known as "least-squares means" For a One-Way ANOVA, this is the same as just looking at the means of our groups. ::: subpoint ○ Will get a bit more complicated with more than just one factor... ::: Useful to report with your ANOVA results to actually see the differences between means. ## Why Estimated Marginal Means These plots all have the same $F$ statistic from a One-Way ANOVA, but their implications are very different! ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell layout-ncol="3" layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-2.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-3.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Estimated Marginal Means Remember those interpretations of slope parameters? :::: {.columns style="font-size:59%"} ::: {.column width="66%"} Dummy coding compares $g-1$ groups to $\beta_0 =$ **reference group mean**: | Predictor | $g_1$ | $g_2$ | $\cdots$ | $g_{G-1}$ | $g_G$ | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | $x_1$ | 1 | 0 | $\cdots$ | 0 | 0 | | $x_2$ | 0 | 1 | $\cdots$ | 0 | 0 | | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | | $x_{G-1}$ | 0 | 0 | $\cdots$ | 1 | 0 | ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Dummy coding:** - $\beta_0: = \mu_3$ - $\beta_1: = \mu_{1} - \mu_3$ - $\beta_2: = \mu_{2} - \mu_3$ ::: :::: :::: {.columns style="font-size:59%"} ::: {.column width="66%"} Effects or contrast coding compares $g-1$ groups to $\beta_0 =$ **grand mean**: | Predictor | $g_1$ | $g_2$ | $\cdots$ | $g_{G-1}$ | $g_G$ | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | $x_1$ | 1 | 0 | $\cdots$ | 0 | -1 | | $x_2$ | 0 | 1 | $\cdots$ | 0 | -1 | | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | | $x_{G-1}$ | 0 | 0 | $\cdots$ | 1 | -1 | ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Contrast/Effects coding:** - $\beta_0: = \mu$ - $\beta_1: = \mu_{1} - \mu$ - $\beta_2: = \mu_{2} - \mu$ Compares groups to **grand mean** ::: :::: The means calculated from the slope parameters are the Estimated Marginal Means (EMMs) as predicted by our model. ::: footer [Stolen from Mark's slides](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/lecture/slides/16%20One%20Way%20ANOVA/Lecture%2016%20One%20Way%20ANOVA_v0.html#/coding-options) ::: ## One-Way ANOVA Recall from last time... ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(palmerpenguins) penguins_cleaned <- penguins |> filter_out(when_any(is.na(flipper_length_mm), is.na(species))) flipper_model <- aov(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) flipper_model_lm <- lm(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) summary(flipper_model); summary(flipper_model_lm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) species 2 52473 26237 594.8 <2e-16 *** Residuals 339 14953 44 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -17.9536 -4.8235 0.0464 4.8130 20.0464 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 189.9536 0.5405 351.454 < 2e-16 *** speciesChinstrap 5.8699 0.9699 6.052 3.79e-09 *** speciesGentoo 27.2333 0.8067 33.760 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 6.642 on 339 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.7782, Adjusted R-squared: 0.7769 F-statistic: 594.8 on 2 and 339 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Let's get the estimated marginal means of penguin flipper length by species! ## EMMs in R To obtain the EMMs for some linear model: `emmeans::emmeans(model, specs)` ::: subpoint ○ `model` = linear model object (e.g., from `lm()`, `aov()`, or `stan_glm()`) ::: ::: subpoint ○ `specs` = predictors for which you want estimated marginal means :::
::: {.callout-note style="font-size:85%"} ### `emmeans` and pipes `|>` While we often want to use pipes in our `R` code, and e.g., might want to plot the EMMs from `emmeans`, the developers explicitly recommend to always **manually check** the output of the `emmeans` function! They provide annotations and context that we will lose if we immediately pipe it into something else (e.g., `emmeans(model, specs) |> as_tibble()`) ::: ## One-Way ANOVA `emmeans` ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("emmeans") library(emmeans) emms_flipper <- emmeans(flipper_model, specs = "species") emms_flipper ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL Adelie 190 0.540 339 189 191 Chinstrap 196 0.805 339 194 197 Gentoo 217 0.599 339 216 218 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Plotting One-Way `emmeans` :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Super quick plotting method with `plot()`. Points are Estimated Marginal Means, and bars are confidence intervals for those EMMs. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(emms_flipper) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Plotting One-Way `emmeans` :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Returns a `ggplot`, so you can work with it from there. But don't have muchhh control over the geometries (`geom`s) or mapping (`mapping = aes()`). Feel free to check out the documentation at [rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/reference/plot.html](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/reference/plot.html) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(emms_flipper) + scale_x_continuous("Estimated Marginal Mean", limits = c(180, 230)) + guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T), y = guide_axis(NULL, cap = T)) + theme_classic(base_size = 14) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Plotting One-Way `emmeans` :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Can also easily make ourselves by converting the `emmeans` object into a `tibble` (again, after we've looked at it ourselves!) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_flipper_df <- as_tibble(emms_flipper) emms_flipper_df |> glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 3 Columns: 6 $ species Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo $ emmean 189.9536, 195.8235, 217.1870 $ SE 0.5404799, 0.8054037, 0.5988465 $ df 339, 339, 339 $ lower.CL 188.8905, 194.2393, 216.0091 $ upper.CL 191.0168, 197.4077, 218.3649 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=2} If plotting point estimates, we always want to include our uncertainty. ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment fragment-index=1 width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_flipper_df |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = emmean)) + geom_point() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Plotting One-Way `emmeans` :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} `geom_errorbar(mapping = aes(x, ymin, ymax), width = 0.9)` ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Alternatively, can specify `aes(y, xmin, xmin)` to flip the other way ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `width` = width of error bar, may want to shrink `width` below its default ::: The correct interpretation of error bars can be ambiguous (one SE? Boo! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](../media/lab_09/anti-hardcoding_1.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](../media/lab_09/anti-hardcoding_2.jpg) ::: :::: ## Effect Size: Dynamically :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="15%"} ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} flipper_model_tidy <- broom::tidy(flipper_model) flipper_model_tidy ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 6 term df sumsq meansq statistic p.value 1 species 2 52473. 26237. 595. 1.35e-111 2 Residuals 339 14953. 44.1 NA NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ms_w <- flipper_model_tidy |> filter(term == "Residuals") |> pull(meansq) df_e <- flipper_model_tidy |> filter(term == "Residuals") |> pull(df) eff_size(emms_flipper, method = "pairwise", edf = df_e, sigma = sqrt(ms_w)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast effect.size SE df lower.CL upper.CL Adelie - Chinstrap -0.884 0.150 339 -1.18 -0.589 Adelie - Gentoo -4.100 0.199 339 -4.49 -3.709 Chinstrap - Gentoo -3.217 0.195 339 -3.60 -2.833 sigma used for effect sizes: 6.642 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="15%"} ::: :::: ![](../media/lab_09/less-remembering.png){.absolute top="15%" right="18%" width="250px" style="transform: rotate(5deg);" .fragment fragment-index=1} ![](../media/lab_09/rounding-errors.png){.absolute bottom="35%" left="0%" width="250px" style="transform: rotate(-14deg);" .fragment fragment-index=1} ![](../media/lab_09/up-to-date.png){.absolute bottom="18%" right="5%" width="250px" style="transform: rotate(17deg);" .fragment fragment-index=1} ## Nice Tables The `gt` package can make excellent tables! ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("gt") library(gt) emms_flipper_df |> gt() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Can examine differences between two groups... or sets of groups. Typically specify *a priori* (planned before data collection), and often have some theoretical reason for doing that contrast ## Setting up a Linear Contrast I Maybe you as a researcher are very interested in Gentoo penguins. You want to compare Gentoo penguins to all other penguin species. ## Setting up a Linear Contrast I {.contrast-slide} ::: {.sub} Species means from the `palmerpenguins` data ::: ::::::::: {.layout} :::::::: {.diagram} ::::::: {.row} [Gentoo]{.cell .big} [Adelie]{.cell .big} [Chinstrap]{.cell .big} ::::::: ::::::: {.row .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="1"} :::::: {.panel .pos} [+]{.sign} [Gentoo]{.cell} []{.eq .ghost} []{.total .ghost} :::::: :::::: {.panel .neg} [−]{.sign} [Adelie]{.cell} []{.op .ghost} [Chinstrap]{.cell} []{.eq .ghost} []{.total .ghost} :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.row .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="2"} :::::: {.panel .pos} [+]{.sign} [$1$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$1$]{.total} :::::: :::::: {.panel .neg} [−]{.sign} [$1$]{.cell} [+]{.op} [$1$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$-2$]{.total} :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.row .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="3"} :::::: {.panel .pos} [+]{.sign} [$\tfrac{1}{1}$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$1$]{.total} :::::: :::::: {.panel .neg} [−]{.sign} [$\tfrac{1}{2}$]{.cell} [+]{.op} [$\tfrac{1}{2}$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$-1$]{.total} :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.row .final .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="4"} [$H_0$:]{.h0} [$(1)\,\mu_{\text{Gentoo}}$]{.cell} [+]{.op} [$\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\mu_{\text{Adelie}}$]{.cell} [+]{.op} [$\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\mu_{\text{Chinstrap}}$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$0$]{.zero} ::::::: :::::::: :::::::: {.notes-col} ::: {.note .n1 .fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="1"} First, here are all of the groups laid out. These represent every we could include in our comparison. ::: ::: {.note .n2 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1"} Next, ask: *which group, or groups, do I want to compare?* If a side contains several groups, they are weighted equally within the comparison. Here, we plan to compare Gentoo penguins with the average of Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. Which side is positive and which is negative is arbitrary; it only affects interpretation. ::: ::: {.note .n3 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2"} Now we need the *weights* on each side to balance, so that everything sums to zero across the selected groups. Right now there is 1 mean on the positive side and 2 on the negative side. If we give every group a weight of 1, the positive side adds up to $1$ and the negative side to $-2$. ::: ::: {.note .n4 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3"} If we divide each side by its total, each side sums to $1$ or $-1$, so the two sides now balance. ::: ::: {.note .n5 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="4"} Our null hypothesis is then that there is no difference between the two sides: the difference between them is zero. ::: :::::::: ::::::::: ## Testing a Linear Contrast I $$ \psi_1 = (1) \ \mu_\text{Gentoo} \ + \ (-\frac{1}{2}) \ \mu_\text{Adelie} \ + \ (-\frac{1}{2}) \ \mu_\text{Chinstrap}$$ **Hypotheses**: $H_0: \psi_1 = 0$ $H_A: \psi_1 \neq 0$ ## Testing a Linear Contrast I ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_flipper ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL Adelie 190 0.540 339 189 191 Chinstrap 196 0.805 339 194 197 Gentoo 217 0.599 339 216 218 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} levels(penguins_cleaned$species) # what order are they in? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Adelie" "Chinstrap" "Gentoo" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} contrast(emms_flipper, method = list(gentoo_vs_others = c(-1/2, -1/2, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value gentoo_vs_others 24.3 0.771 339 31.532 <0.0001 ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment There is a significant difference between Gentoo flipper length and the average of Adelie and Chinstrap flipper lengths. ::: ## Setting up a Linear Contrast II You don't have to include all groups in a contrasts' comparison. "Zero-out" a group in a contrast equation by setting its weight to zero. For example, let's just compare Gentoo penguins to Adelie penguins. ## Setting up a Linear Contrast II {.contrast-slide} ::: {.sub} Just comparing Gentoo and Adelie penguins. ::: ::::::::: {.layout} :::::::: {.diagram .three} ::::::: {.row} [Gentoo]{.cell .big} [Adelie]{.cell .big} [Chinstrap]{.cell .big} ::::::: ::::::: {.row .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="1"} :::::: {.panel .pos} [+]{.sign} [Gentoo]{.cell} []{.eq .ghost} []{.total .ghost} :::::: :::::: {.panel .neg} [−]{.sign} [Adelie]{.cell} []{.eq .ghost} []{.total .ghost} :::::: :::::: {.panel .nul} [0]{.sign} [Chinstrap]{.cell} []{.eq .ghost} []{.total .ghost} :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.row .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="2"} :::::: {.panel .pos} [+]{.sign} [$1$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$1$]{.total} :::::: :::::: {.panel .neg} [−]{.sign} [$1$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$-1$]{.total} :::::: :::::: {.panel .nul} [0]{.sign} [$0$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$0$]{.total} :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.row .final .fragment .fade-up data-fragment-index="3"} [$H_0$:]{.h0} [$(1)\,\mu_{\text{Gentoo}}$]{.cell} [+]{.op} [$(-1)\,\mu_{\text{Adelie}}$]{.cell} [+]{.op} [$(0)\,\mu_{\text{Chinstrap}}$]{.cell} [=]{.eq} [$0$]{.zero} ::::::: :::::::: :::::::: {.notes-col} ::: {.note .n1 .fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="1"} We still have all the groups available to us, but this time we only want to compare Gentoo and Adelie ::: ::: {.note .n2 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1"} To do this, Chinstrap gets "zero-ed out". We will assign it a weight of zero. ::: ::: {.note .n3 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2"} Since Chinstrap's coefficient is zero, we don't have to consider it in our "sum to zero" constraint. ::: ::: {.note .n4 .fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3"} We only have one group on each (positive / negative) side, so we don't have to divide here. Implicitly, we are dividing each by one. ::: :::::::: ::::::::: ## Testing a Linear Contrast II $$ \begin{aligned} \psi_2 &= (1) \ \mu_\text{Gentoo} \ + \ (-1) \ \mu_\text{Adelie} \ + \ (0) \ \mu_\text{Chinstrap} \\ &= (1) \ \mu_\text{Gentoo} \ + \ (-1) \ \mu_\text{Adelie} \\ &= \mu_\text{Gentoo} - \mu_\text{Adelie} \end{aligned} $$ **Hypotheses**: $H_0: \psi_2 = 0$ $H_A: \psi_2 \neq 0$ ## Testing a Linear Contrast II ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_flipper ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL Adelie 190 0.540 339 189 191 Chinstrap 196 0.805 339 194 197 Gentoo 217 0.599 339 216 218 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} contrast(emms_flipper, method = list(gentoo_vs_adelie = c(-1, 0, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value gentoo_vs_adelie 27.2 0.807 339 33.760 <0.0001 ``` ::: ::: ## Polynomial Contrasts If your groups have some natural *ordering* and *equal intervals* between levels, you may also be interested in testing a polynomial contrast. Polynomial contrasts tests for polynomial relationships in the outcome. If you have $J$ groups, you can test for $J-1$ polynomial contrasts, e.g., :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Linear** ($J \geq2$) $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-34-1.svg){width=192} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Quadratic** ($J \geq 3$) $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.svg){width=192} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Cubic** ($J \geq 4$) $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2x^2 + \beta_3x^3$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.svg){width=192} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Polynomial Contrasts Polynomial contrasts use pre-specified weights for each term ($x$, $x^2$, $x^3$, etc.), e.g., ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

We have three groups (year = 2007, 2008, 2009), with ordered, equal spaced intervals between groups, so we can fit a linear and quadratic contrast. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_year_data <- penguins |> mutate(year = factor(year, ordered = T)) year_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ year, data = penguins_year_data) summary(year_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = body_mass_g ~ year, data = penguins_year_data) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1566.7 -666.7 -174.5 547.8 2175.5 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 4200.50 43.41 96.770 <2e-16 *** year.L 60.64 75.21 0.806 0.421 year.Q -81.04 75.16 -1.078 0.282 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 802.2 on 339 degrees of freedom (2 observations deleted due to missingness) Multiple R-squared: 0.005193, Adjusted R-squared: -0.000676 F-statistic: 0.8848 on 2 and 339 DF, p-value: 0.4137 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emms_year <- emmeans(year_model, specs = "year") emms_year ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` year emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL 2007 4125 76.8 339 3973 4276 2008 4267 75.1 339 4119 4414 2009 4210 73.5 339 4066 4355 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} contrast(emms_year, method = "poly") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value linear 85.8 106 339 0.806 0.4207 quadratic -198.5 184 339 -1.078 0.2817 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: ## Polynomial Contrasts We found no significant linear or quadratic effect of year on penguin body mass. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_09_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # I had Claude Sonnet 5.5 Low make this plot on 2026-10-23. P <- contr.poly(3) m <- emms_year_df$emmean gm <- mean(m) fits <- tibble( year = emms_year_df$year, Linear = gm + sum(P[, 1] * m) * P[, 1], Quadratic = gm + sum(P[, 2] * m) * P[, 2] ) |> pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "poly", values_to = "fit") emms_year_df |> ggplot(aes(x = year, y = emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL, color = year)) + geom_violin(data = penguins_year_data, aes(x = year, y = body_mass_g, fill = year), alpha = 0.2, color = NA, inherit.aes = F) + geom_jitter(data = penguins_year_data, aes(x = year, y = body_mass_g, color = year), alpha = 0.15, shape = 21, size = 1.5, inherit.aes = F) + # Theoretical polynomial fits geom_line(data = fits, aes(x = year, y = fit, group = poly, linetype = poly), color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.8, inherit.aes = F) + geom_point(data = fits, aes(x = year, y = fit, shape = poly), color = "grey25", fill = "white", size = 2.5, inherit.aes = F) + # Observed EMMs geom_errorbar(width = 0.1) + geom_point() + scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = c(Linear = "dashed", Quadratic = "dotted")) + scale_shape_manual(NULL, values = c(Linear = 22, Quadratic = 24)) + scale_x_discrete("Year") + scale_y_continuous("EMM of Body Mass (g)") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(2500, 6500)) + labs(caption = "Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.") + guides(x = guide_axis(NULL, cap = T), y = guide_axis(cap = T), color = "none", fill = "none") + theme_classic() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: ::: ## Polynomial Contrasts

  (function () {

      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
